claim: The apicoplast is a four-membrane plastid found in the apicomplexans.
source: The apicoplast is a four-membrane plastid found in the apicomplexans, which harbors biosynthesis and organelle housekeeping activities in the matrix.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the apicoplast structure.

claim: The apicoplast harbors biosynthesis and organelle housekeeping activities in the matrix.
source: The apicoplast is a four-membrane plastid found in the apicomplexans, which harbors biosynthesis and organelle housekeeping activities in the matrix.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of the apicoplast.

claim: The mechanism driving the flux of metabolites in and out of the apicoplast remains unknown.
source: However, the mechanism driving the flux of metabolites, in and out, remains unknown.
evidence: This statement in the abstract identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: TurboID and genome engineering were used to identify apicoplast transporters in Toxoplasma gondii.
source: Here, we used TurboID and genome engineering to identify apicoplast transporters in Toxoplasma gondii.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study as stated in the abstract.

claim: One pair of apicomplexan monocarboxylate transporters (AMTs) appears to have evolved from a putative host cell that engulfed a red alga.
source: Among the many novel transporters, we show that one pair of apicomplexan monocarboxylate transporters (AMTs) appears to have evolved from a putative host cell that engulfed a red alga.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract based on evolutionary analysis.

claim: AMT1 and AMT2 are critical for parasite growth.
source: Protein depletion showed that AMT1 and AMT2 are critical for parasite growth.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by protein depletion experiments.

claim: AMT1 and AMT2 are associated with biosynthesis of isoprenoids and fatty acids.
source: Metabolite analyses supported the notion that AMT1 and AMT2 are associated with biosynthesis of isoprenoids and fatty acids.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by metabolite analysis data.

claim: Stronger phenotypic defects were observed for AMT2 compared to AMT1.
source: However, stronger phenotypic defects were observed for AMT2, including in the inability to establish T. gondii parasite virulence in mice.
evidence: This comparative finding is stated in the abstract.

claim: AMT2 depletion results in inability to establish T. gondii parasite virulence in mice.
source: However, stronger phenotypic defects were observed for AMT2, including in the inability to establish T. gondii parasite virulence in mice.
evidence: This is a specific phenotypic outcome stated in the abstract.

claim: Apicomplexan evolution included two key independent and sequential endosymbiotic events.
source: It is believed that apicomplexan evolution included two key independent, and sequential, endosymbiotic events, finally leading to the common ancestor of the chromalveolates (e.g. alveolates, heterokonts, oomycetes, and Cryptomonads) (Cavalier-Smith, 1999; Gould et al., 2008; Janouskovec et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The apicoplast originates from a red alga.
source: Though endosymbiont origins of the apicoplast were proposed (Köhler et al., 1997; McFadden et al., 1996; Wilson et al., 1996), it is believed that the apicoplast originates from a red alga (Foth and McFadden, 2003; McFadden and van Dooren, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The apicoplast membranes have been proposed to evolve from the red algal plastid, the algal plasma membrane, and the host endomembrane.
source: Therefore, the apicoplast membranes have been proposed to evolve from the red algal plastid, the algal plasma membrane, and the host endomembrane when counting from the innermost to outermost membranes of the apicoplast (Gould et al., 2008; McFadden and Yeh, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The apicoplast houses the fatty acid synthesis type II (FASII) pathway.
source: These pathways include the fatty acid synthesis type II (FASII) pathway, methylerythritol phosphate (MEP) pathway, Fe–S cluster biosynthesis pathway, (partial) heme biosynthesis pathway, and lysophosphatidic acid synthesis pathway (using the FASII products) (Amiar et al., 2016; Fata and Rabuzzi, 1988; Jomaa et al., 1999; Kloehn et al., 2021; Ralph et al., 2004; Tjhin et al., 2020; Waller et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The apicoplast houses the methylerythritol phosphate (MEP) pathway.
source: These pathways include the fatty acid synthesis type II (FASII) pathway, methylerythritol phosphate (MEP) pathway, Fe–S cluster biosynthesis pathway, (partial) heme biosynthesis pathway, and lysophosphatidic acid synthesis pathway (using the FASII products) (Amiar et al., 2016; Fata and Rabuzzi, 1988; Jomaa et al., 1999; Kloehn et al., 2021; Ralph et al., 2004; Tjhin et al., 2020; Waller et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The apicoplast houses the Fe–S cluster biosynthesis pathway.
source: These pathways include the fatty acid synthesis type II (FASII) pathway, methylerythritol phosphate (MEP) pathway, Fe–S cluster biosynthesis pathway, (partial) heme biosynthesis pathway, and lysophosphatidic acid synthesis pathway (using the FASII products) (Amiar et al., 2016; Fata and Rabuzzi, 1988; Jomaa et al., 1999; Kloehn et al., 2021; Ralph et al., 2004; Tjhin et al., 2020; Waller et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The apicoplast houses the (partial) heme biosynthesis pathway.
source: These pathways include the fatty acid synthesis type II (FASII) pathway, methylerythritol phosphate (MEP) pathway, Fe–S cluster biosynthesis pathway, (partial) heme biosynthesis pathway, and lysophosphatidic acid synthesis pathway (using the FASII products) (Amiar et al., 2016; Fata and Rabuzzi, 1988; Jomaa et al., 1999; Kloehn et al., 2021; Ralph et al., 2004; Tjhin et al., 2020; Waller et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The apicoplast houses the lysophosphatidic acid synthesis pathway.
source: These pathways include the fatty acid synthesis type II (FASII) pathway, methylerythritol phosphate (MEP) pathway, Fe–S cluster biosynthesis pathway, (partial) heme biosynthesis pathway, and lysophosphatidic acid synthesis pathway (using the FASII products) (Amiar et al., 2016; Fata and Rabuzzi, 1988; Jomaa et al., 1999; Kloehn et al., 2021; Ralph et al., 2004; Tjhin et al., 2020; Waller et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The apicoplast FASII pathway in T. gondii can become essential under metabolic adaptation conditions.
source: The apicoplast FASII pathway in T. gondii is key to understand the metabolic flexibility, and can become essential under metabolic adaptation conditions (Amiar et al., 2020; Botté et al., 2013; Krishnan et al., 2020; Primo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The apicoplast maintains housekeeping activities for genome replication, transcription, and translation.
source: Moreover, the apicoplast maintains housekeeping activities for genome replication, transcription, and translation (Low et al., 2018; McFadden and Roos, 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The nature of the channels and transporters in the apicoplast remains obscure compared to plant plastids.
source: However, compared to plant plastids, the nature of the channels and transporters in the apicoplast remains obscure.
evidence: This statement in the introduction identifies a knowledge gap.

claim: TgAPT1 is a phosphate translocator in T. gondii.
source: A similar approach was utilized to identify phosphate translocators in T. gondii (i.e. TgAPT1) and P. falciparum (i.e. PfiTPT and PfoTPT), and a two-pore channel TPC in T. gondii.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing previously identified transporters.

claim: PfiTPT and PfoTPT are phosphate translocators in P. falciparum.
source: A similar approach was utilized to identify phosphate translocators in T. gondii (i.e. TgAPT1) and P. falciparum (i.e. PfiTPT and PfoTPT), and a two-pore channel TPC in T. gondii.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing previously identified transporters.

claim: TPC is a two-pore channel in T. gondii.
source: A similar approach was utilized to identify phosphate translocators in T. gondii (i.e. TgAPT1) and P. falciparum (i.e. PfiTPT and PfoTPT), and a two-pore channel TPC in T. gondii.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing previously identified transporters.

claim: These transporters are capable of supplying phosphorylated carbons and calcium to the apicoplast.
source: These transporters are capable of supplying phosphorylated carbons (Brooks et al., 2010; Fleige et al., 2007; Karnataki et al., 2007; Lim et al., 2010; Mullin et al., 2006), and calcium to the apicoplast (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: 57–58% of the chloroplast transporters have an origin in the putative host cell in the first endosymbiosis.
source: Consistent with that, studies demonstrated that 57–58% of the chloroplast transporters have an origin in the putative host cell in the first endosymbiosis while 20–30% are from bacteria (Karkar et al., 2015; Tyra et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: 20–30% of chloroplast transporters are from bacteria.
source: Consistent with that, studies demonstrated that 57–58% of the chloroplast transporters have an origin in the putative host cell in the first endosymbiosis while 20–30% are from bacteria (Karkar et al., 2015; Tyra et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The major source of pyruvate required for the biosynthesis pathways in the apicoplast of T. gondii and P. falciparum is still unknown.
source: Recent studies suggested that we still do not know the major source of pyruvate required for the biosynthesis pathways in the apicoplast of T. gondii and P. falciparum (Swift et al., 2020; Xia et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The hyperplexed localization of organelle proteins (hyperLOPIT) assigned 129 proteins to the apicoplast.
source: The hyperplexed localization of organelle proteins (hyperLOPIT) assigned 129 proteins to the apicoplast (Barylyuk et al., 2020), of which three proteins were likely transporters, that is APT1 (transmembrane domain, TMD = 6), one major facilitator superfamily (MFS) transporter (TGME49_309580) (HAP1, hypothetical apicoplast protein 1), and one hypothetical protein (TGME49_267690) (HAP2) (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the hyperLOPIT dataset.

claim: Three proteins from hyperLOPIT were likely transporters: APT1, one MFS transporter (HAP1), and one hypothetical protein (HAP2).
source: The hyperplexed localization of organelle proteins (hyperLOPIT) assigned 129 proteins to the apicoplast (Barylyuk et al., 2020), of which three proteins were likely transporters, that is APT1 (transmembrane domain, TMD = 6), one major facilitator superfamily (MFS) transporter (TGME49_309580) (HAP1, hypothetical apicoplast protein 1), and one hypothetical protein (TGME49_267690) (HAP2) (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the hyperLOPIT dataset.

claim: An apicoplast proteomic dataset obtained by BioID fusion at ACP in P. falciparum reported 16 TMDs ≥6 protein candidates.
source: We also mined an apicoplast proteomic dataset obtained by the BioID fusion at acyl carrier protein (ACP) in P. falciparum (Boucher et al., 2018), which reported 16 TMDs ≥6 protein candidates, and two additional candidates annotated as ABC transporters (TMDs <6).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the ACP-BioID dataset.

claim: Eight orthologs in T. gondii were identified from the P. falciparum candidates and temporarily named as HAP3–9.
source: We identified the orthologs in T. gondii using the P. falciparum candidates (Boucher et al., 2018; Sayers et al., 2018), resulting in eight candidates in T. gondii. They were temporarily named as HAP3–9 (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the identification of orthologs.

claim: APT1 was reported to mainly localize to four of the apicoplast membranes by immuno-EM.
source: Though the streptavidin signal and the protein itself were slightly diffused (Karnataki et al., 2007), APT1 was reported to mainly localize to four of the apicoplast membranes by an immuno-electron microscopy (immuno-EM) approach for HA epitopes tagged at the C-terminus of APT1 (Karnataki et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: APT1 itself has the highest p-value associated with its enrichment in the TurboID line.
source: This analysis showed that APT1 itself has the highest p-value associated with its enrichment in the TurboID line, as would be expected for a bait protein.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: Fifteen novel apicoplast membrane proteins were identified in T. gondii.
source: Of the 15 novel apicoplast membrane proteins, we identified in T. gondii that 12 proteins are annotated as putative transporters or carriers in TOXODB, and 3 are annotated as hypothetical proteins (TMD ≥6) (Figure 1F and Supplementary file 2f).
evidence: This is stated in the results section summarizing the screening results.

claim: Twelve of the 15 novel apicoplast membrane proteins are annotated as putative transporters or carriers in TOXODB.
source: Of the 15 novel apicoplast membrane proteins, we identified in T. gondii that 12 proteins are annotated as putative transporters or carriers in TOXODB, and 3 are annotated as hypothetical proteins (TMD ≥6) (Figure 1F and Supplementary file 2f).
evidence: This is stated in the results section summarizing the screening results.

claim: Three of the 15 novel apicoplast membrane proteins are annotated as hypothetical proteins (TMD ≥6).
source: Of the 15 novel apicoplast membrane proteins, we identified in T. gondii that 12 proteins are annotated as putative transporters or carriers in TOXODB, and 3 are annotated as hypothetical proteins (TMD ≥6) (Figure 1F and Supplementary file 2f).
evidence: This is stated in the results section summarizing the screening results.

claim: One novel protein was from hyperLOPIT, 3 from ACP-BirA, and 14 from APT1-TurboID.
source: These novel proteins included 1 from hyperLOPIT, 3 from ACP-BirA, and 14 from our APT1-TurboID (Figure 1G), among which three of these proteins were shared between the APT1-TurboID and the combinations of hyperLOPIT and ACP-BirA (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section summarizing the sources of novel proteins.

claim: Three proteins were shared between the APT1-TurboID and the combinations of hyperLOPIT and ACP-BirA.
source: These novel proteins included 1 from hyperLOPIT, 3 from ACP-BirA, and 14 from our APT1-TurboID (Figure 1G), among which three of these proteins were shared between the APT1-TurboID and the combinations of hyperLOPIT and ACP-BirA (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section summarizing the sources of novel proteins.

claim: Most novel transporters were likely to be derived from the endosymbiont.
source: Their conservation, including in plastid-deficient taxa, that is Gregarina and Cryptosporidia, indicates that these proteins were relics of the former plastid in evolution via endosymbiont gene transfers (Gould et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on conservation analysis.

claim: The pair of MCTs (AMT1 and AMT2) may have an origin in a heterotrophic protist – the putative host cell.
source: In sharp contrast, the pair of MCTs (AMT1 and AMT2) may have an origin in a heterotrophic protist – the putative host cell.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on evolutionary analysis.

claim: AMT1-6Ty was almost perfectly co-localized with AMT2-6HA.
source: The confocal imaging showed that AMT1-6Ty was almost perfectly co-localized with AMT2-6HA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that the putative transporters are highly likely to be localized at the apicoplast membranes.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by confocal imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Immuno-EM provided evidence supporting the membrane localization of AMT1 and AMT2.
source: In support of this model, immuno-EM provided a further piece of evidence, supporting the membrane localization of AMT1 and AMT2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immuno-EM data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The AID fusions were efficiently and stably depleted in IAA treatments for 3–36 hr.
source: As expected, the AID fusions were efficiently and stably depleted in IAA treatments for 3–36 hr, as shown on western blots (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 3A.

claim: Western blots detected two bands in the single and double AID fusion lines, which might be the precursor and mature forms of AMT1 and AMT2.
source: It was noteworthy that western blots detected two bands in the single and double AID fusion lines, which might be the precursor and mature forms of AMT1 and AMT2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 3A.

claim: The AID lines grown in IAA did not form discernible plaques.
source: We observed that the AID lines grown in IAA did not form discernible plaques (Figure 3C), which was supported by further analysis of the plaque numbers and areas (Figure 3D, E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by plaque assay data in Figure 3C, D, E.

claim: Parasite replication was significantly affected in the first 24 hr of growth and became worse in the following cycles of 24 hr.
source: Using IFA analysis of the parasites, we observed that parasite replication was significantly affected in the first 24 hr of growth and became worse in the following cycles of 24 hr, especially the 3rd 24-hr period (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by replication assay data in Figure 3F.

claim: ACP partially diffused in the cytosol of intracellular parasites grown in IAA for 24 hr.
source: We observed that ACP partially diffused in the cytosol of intracellular parasites grown in IAA for 24 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), whereas it completely diffused in the cytosol of extracellular parasites that had grown in IAA for 24 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by IFA data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: ACP completely diffused in the cytosol of extracellular parasites that had grown in IAA for 24 hr.
source: We observed that ACP partially diffused in the cytosol of intracellular parasites grown in IAA for 24 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), whereas it completely diffused in the cytosol of extracellular parasites that had grown in IAA for 24 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by IFA data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Depletion of AMT2-AID resulted in much more severe defects (swelling or breakdown) of the apicoplast than that of AMT1-AID.
source: These results suggested that depletion of AMT2-AID resulted in much more severe defects (swelling or breakdown) of the apicoplast than that of AMT1-AID, and further depletion of AMT1-AID had no further effect.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on ACP diffusion analysis.

claim: GFP transport to the VAC following its uptake from host cell cytosol is dependent on protein prenylation of Rab1B and YKT6.1.
source: Our recent data showed that GFP transport to the VAC following its uptake from host cell cytosol is dependent on protein prenylation of Rab1B and YKT6.1 (Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The GFP vesicles diffused through the cytosol and were unable to accumulate at the VAC in the AID parasites grown in IAA.
source: In contrast, the GFP vesicles diffused through the cytosol, and were unable to accumulate at the VAC in the AID parasites grown in IAA with the absence/presence of atorvastatin, as shown by significantly reduced percentages (~8%) of the parasites in the AID lines induced for 12 hr (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by GFP acquisition assay data in Figure 4B.

claim: Depletion of AMT1-AID and AMT2-AID showed a strong defect of reduced protein abundance of Rab1B.
source: We further tested Rab1B stability in the AMT-AID lines grown in IAA for 12 hr, which showed a strong defect of reduced protein abundance of Rab1B by scoring of parasites with normal or abnormal level of Rab1B using an IFA approach (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by IFA data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Parasites depleted with AMT1-AID and AMT2-AID had similar levels of reduced GFP transport at 12 hr of IAA induction.
source: However, it was noteworthy that parasites depleted with AMT1-AID and AMT2-AID had similar levels of reduced GFP transport and parasites with reduced protein abundance of Rab1B at the 12 hr of IAA induction, suggesting that depletions of AMT1 and AMT2 resulted in similar levels of IPP reduction in parasites.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on GFP transport assay data.

claim: Three AID lines shared 13 differential metabolites.
source: Interestingly, three AID lines shared 13 differential metabolites (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by metabolomics data in Figure 4C.

claim: The shared metabolites included fatty acids and lipids, such as myristic acid, palmitoleic acid, trans-oleic acid, and phospholipids containing C14 and C18 fatty acids.
source: The shared metabolites included fatty acids and lipids, such as myristic acid (C14 fatty acid), palmitoleic acid (C16 fatty acid), trans-oleic acid (C18 fatty acid), and phospholipids containing C14 and C18 fatty acids (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by metabolomics data in Figure 4D, E.

claim: Depletion of the transporters significantly impaired the de novo biosynthesis of fatty acids by the FASII activity in the parasite.
source: We then concluded that depletion of the transporters significantly impaired the de novo biosynthesis of fatty acids by the FASII activity in the parasite.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on metabolomics data.

claim: The metabolomics also identified metabolites related to the TCA cycle, such as gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), glutamic acid, and succinic acid.
source: Intriguingly, the metabolomics also identified metabolites related to the TCA cycle, such as gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), glutamic acid, and succinic acid (Figure 4E), which were shared among three of the AID lines.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by metabolomics data in Figure 4E.

claim: ACC1 was found to be gone only in the AMT2-AID parasites, but not in the AMT1-AID parasites, upon protein depletion in IAA for 36 hr.
source: Upon protein depletion in IAA for 36 hr, ACC1 was found to be gone only in the AMT2-AID parasites, but not in the AMT1-AID parasites, as demonstrated by western blots (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 5C.

claim: Only ~40% of the vacuoles contained one or two parasites with ACC1 signal in AMT2-AID parasites.
source: The quantification assay showed that only ~40% of the vacuoles contained one or two parasites with ACC1 signal (types 2 and 3) (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by quantification data in Figure 5F.

claim: ACC1 in those parasites was still biotinylated, as shown in streptavidin stains.
source: However, ACC1 in those parasites was still biotinylated, as shown in streptavidin stains (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by IFA data in Figure 5G.

claim: AMT2 is associated with stability of ACC1 in a way, as yet, unknown, but unrelated with biotin availability in the apicoplast.
source: Collectively, AMT2 is associated with stability of ACC1 in a way, as yet, unknown, but unrelated with biotin availability in the apicoplast.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on ACC1 analysis.

claim: The four membranes surrounding the apicoplast remained visible, but were loosened, and the interior of the organelle appeared less dense and even electron lucent in the AID parasites induced for 24 hr.
source: The transmission electron microscopy (TEM) demonstrated that the four membranes surrounding the apicoplast remained visible, but were loosened, and the interior of the organelle appeared less dense and even electron lucent in the AID parasites, which had been induced for 24 hr in comparison with the TIR1 parasites (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by TEM data in Figure 6A.

claim: Depletion of AMT1 caused modest loss of the apicoplast.
source: These results suggested that depletion of AMT1 caused modest loss of the apicoplast, yet the AMT2 depletion appeared to have a greater effect on the apicoplast loss.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on TEM quantification data.

claim: AMT2 depletion appeared to have a greater effect on the apicoplast loss.
source: These results suggested that depletion of AMT1 caused modest loss of the apicoplast, yet the AMT2 depletion appeared to have a greater effect on the apicoplast loss.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on TEM quantification data.

claim: Mice infected with TIR1 succumbed to lethal toxoplasmosis by day 10 post infection.
source: Those mice infected with TIR1 succumbed to lethal toxoplasmosis by day 10 post infection (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by survival curve data in Figure 6C.

claim: IAA treatment ultimately prevented acute virulence caused by the parasite lines with the AMT2 depletion (i.e. AMT2-AID and dKD).
source: Conversely, the IAA treatment ultimately prevented acute virulence caused by the parasite lines with the AMT2 depletion (i.e. AMT2-AID and dKD), and it postponed mouse death by the AMT1-AID depletion.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on mouse infection data.

claim: IAA treatment postponed mouse death by the AMT1-AID depletion.
source: Conversely, the IAA treatment ultimately prevented acute virulence caused by the parasite lines with the AMT2 depletion (i.e. AMT2-AID and dKD), and it postponed mouse death by the AMT1-AID depletion.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on mouse infection data.

claim: AMT1-AID was efficiently degraded in mice by the treatment of IAA in only 24 hr.
source: It was clear that AMT1-AID was efficiently degraded in mice by the treatment of IAA in only 24 hr (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by IFA data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: AMT2 was obviously essential for establishing T. gondii infection and virulence in mice.
source: Collectively, AMT2 was obviously essential for establishing T. gondii infection and virulence in mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on mouse infection data.

claim: Most of the apicomplexan parasites harbor a vestigial plastid which undergoes several fitness-conferring or essential metabolic pathways in the matrix.
source: Most of the apicomplexan parasites, such as T. gondii and Plasmodium spp., harbor a vestigial plastid, which undergoes several fitness-conferring or essential metabolic pathways in the matrix (Kloehn et al., 2021; Lim and McFadden, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The transporters that are responsible for exchanging metabolites between the apicoplast and the parasite remain elusive.
source: However, the transporters that are responsible for exchanging metabolites between the apicoplast and the parasite remain elusive, due to difficulties in identification of those transporters in the multiple membranes that surround the organelle.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion identifying a knowledge gap.

claim: Several novel transporters in the apicoplast were discovered using available data and high-efficiency approaches in T. gondii.
source: Here, we fully exploited the currently available data, and the high-efficiency of proximity biotin labeling and CRISPR-Cas9 tagging approaches in the model apicomplexan T. gondii, and discovered several novel transporters in the apicoplast.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the study's approach.

claim: Most of the novel transporters appear to be derived from the endosymbiont (i.e. a red alga) in the evolution of the secondary plastid.
source: Among those putative transporters, most of them appear to be derived from the endosymbiont (i.e. a red alga) in the evolution of the secondary plastid, and only the pair of MCTs AMT1 and AMT2 is likely to be derived from the putative host cell that originally engulfed the endosymbiont.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on evolutionary analysis.

claim: Only the pair of MCTs AMT1 and AMT2 is likely to be derived from the putative host cell that originally engulfed the endosymbiont.
source: Among those putative transporters, most of them appear to be derived from the endosymbiont (i.e. a red alga) in the evolution of the secondary plastid, and only the pair of MCTs AMT1 and AMT2 is likely to be derived from the putative host cell that originally engulfed the endosymbiont.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on evolutionary analysis.

claim: Protein depletion of AMT1 and AMT2 using the TIR1-AID system resulted in defects of plaque formation in vitro, ACP diffusion/apicoplast loss and biosynthetic pathways of the MEP and FASII.
source: Protein depletion of the AMT1 and AMT2 using a highly efficient technique, the TIR1-AID system, resulted in defects of plaque formation in vitro, ACP diffusion/apicoplast loss and biosynthetic pathways of the MEP and FASII.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the phenotypic results.

claim: Depletion of AMT2 clearly caused stronger defects including ACP diffusion/apicoplast loss, FASII produced fatty acids, ACC1 stability and removal of mouse virulence.
source: However, depletion of AMT2 clearly caused stronger defects including ACP diffusion/apicoplast loss, FASII produced fatty acids, ACC1 stability and removal of mouse virulence.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the comparative phenotypic results.

claim: Complex transporting functions are likely to exist in the apicoplast involving AMT1 and AMT2.
source: These results indicate that complex transporting functions are likely to exist in the apicoplast involving AMT1 and AMT2.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the results.

claim: The metabolic integration of the primary plastid was mainly driven by targeting transporters from a heterotrophic protist – the host cell, but not from the endosymbiont – cyanobacteria.
source: Studies suggested that the metabolic integration of the primary plastid (e.g. chloroplast) was mainly driven by targeting transporters from a heterotrophic protist – the host cell, but not from the endosymbiont – cyanobacteria (Karkar et al., 2015; Tyra et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The pair of AMTs may play critical roles in the metabolic integration of the algal endosymbiont into the parasites.
source: This observation therefore provides a perspective that the pair of AMTs may play critical roles in the metabolic integration of the algal endosymbiont into the parasites.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the evolutionary analysis.

claim: Depletion of the transporters AMT1 and AMT2 caused strong defects on plaque formation and parasite replication.
source: Our phenotypic analysis showed that depletion of the transporters AMT1 and AMT2 caused strong defects on plaque formation and parasite replication, suggesting that both transporters are critical on the apicoplast membranes.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the phenotypic results.

claim: Both transporters AMT1 and AMT2 are critical on the apicoplast membranes.
source: Our phenotypic analysis showed that depletion of the transporters AMT1 and AMT2 caused strong defects on plaque formation and parasite replication, suggesting that both transporters are critical on the apicoplast membranes.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the phenotypic results.

claim: Depletion of AMT2 always caused stronger defects in ACP diffusion, FASII fatty acids, apicoplast loss, and mouse virulence.
source: However, we observed disparate degrees of phenotypic disruption in the AMT1- and AMT2-depleted parasites. Depletion of AMT2 always caused stronger defects in ACP diffusion, FASII fatty acids, apicoplast loss, and mouse virulence.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the comparative phenotypic results.

claim: AMT2 is additionally associated with loss of ACC1, a key enzyme for FASII, found in the majority of parasites in a vacuole.
source: AMT2 is additionally associated with loss of ACC1, a key enzyme for FASII, found in the majority of parasites in a vacuole, likely providing another piece of evidence to explain the greater phenotypic defects.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the ACC1 results.

claim: Depletion of FASII enzymes led to loss of apicoplast.
source: Genetic studies suggest that depletion of FASII enzymes led to loss of apicoplast (Liang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The pair of AMTs is likely to transport pyruvate, lactate, amino acids, and other substrates based on knowledge of MCTs.
source: Based on knowledge of MCTs (Felmlee et al., 2020), the pair of AMTs is likely to transport pyruvate, lactate, amino acids, and other substrates.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation based on MCT knowledge.

claim: Pyruvate is the central metabolite that connects many metabolic pathways in living organisms.
source: Pyruvate is the central metabolite that connects many metabolic pathways in living organisms.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as general knowledge.

claim: Pyruvate must be imported into organelles for specific metabolic pathways.
source: It must be imported into organelles for specific metabolic pathways, as suggested with pyruvate import by the NHD1/Bass2-protein coupling function in the chloroplast of C4 plants, and by the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (Bricker et al., 2012; Furumoto, 2016; Furumoto et al., 2011; Gasperotti et al., 2020; Herzig et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Pyruvate is one of the key carbon sources for the condensation with triose phosphates to initiate the biosynthesis pathway of MEP in the parasite.
source: Pyruvate is one of the key carbon sources for the condensation with triose phosphates to initiate the biosynthesis pathway of MEP in the parasite.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as knowledge about the MEP pathway.

claim: Pyruvate is the only carbon source in the FASII pathway for biosynthesis of fatty acids.
source: Meanwhile, pyruvate is the only carbon source in the FASII pathway for biosynthesis of fatty acids (Brooks et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The possible role on pyruvate import by the AMTs could provide a good explanation for the defects on MEP and FASII pathways.
source: The possible role on pyruvate import by the AMTs could provide a good explanation for the defects on MEP and FASII pathways, specifically, the phenotypes reflecting the reduced levels of IPP synthesis in the AMT-depleted parasites.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation about AMT function.

claim: This study successfully identifies several novel apicoplast transporters.
source: Our work successfully identifies several novel apicoplast transporters, thus greatly unraveling the mystery of the apicoplast membrane composition and opening up possibilities to tackle difficult questions about metabolite transport in the apicomplexans.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the study's contribution.

claim: The pair of MCTs AMT1 and AMT2 are likely derived from the putative host cell that engulfed a red algal during the evolution of this group of parasites.
source: The most intriguingly findings in this study are the identification of the pair of MCTs AMT1 and AMT2, which are likely derived from the putative host cell that engulfed a red algal during the evolution of this group of parasites.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing a key finding.

claim: Metabolic analysis together with other phenotypic analyses supported the notion that the pair of AMTs is associated with the MEP and FASII biosynthesis pathways.
source: Metabolic analysis together with other phenotypic analyses supported the notion that the pair of AMTs is associated with the MEP and FASII biosynthesis pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the study's findings.

claim: The phenotypic defects differ greatly between AMT1 and AMT2, supporting a complex function for AMT2 in the apicoplast.
source: However, though both transporters belong to the MCTs, the phenotypic defects differ greatly, supporting a complex function for AMT2 in the apicoplast, however, the substrates transported by the AMTs still await further clarification.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the comparative results.

claim: The substrates transported by the AMTs still await further clarification.
source: However, though both transporters belong to the MCTs, the phenotypic defects differ greatly, supporting a complex function for AMT2 in the apicoplast, however, the substrates transported by the AMTs still await further clarification.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion identifying a limitation.

claim: The MCTs are likely to control similar essential processes in related protists, especially in other members of this phylum of deadly parasites.
source: Collectively, the MCTs are likely to control similar essential processes in related protists, especially in other members of this phylum of deadly parasites.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a broader implication of the findings.

claim: APT1-TurboID enriched apicoplast proteins as shown by the volcano map analysis.
source: This analysis showed that APT1 itself has the highest p-value associated with its enrichment in the TurboID line, as would be expected for a bait protein. The TMD candidates (TMD ≥6 and 2 ≤ TMD < 6) were evenly distributed on the volcano map plotted by fold changes against p-values in a similar pattern to the distribution of known apicoplast proteins (Figure 1C and Supplementary file 2c). These features suggested that APT1-TurboID had enriched apicoplast proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the volcano map analysis showing enrichment patterns in Figure 1C.

claim: The apicoplast acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1 (ACC1) is a strongly biotinylated protein.
source: The apicoplast acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1 (ACC1) is a strongly biotinylated protein (Zuther et al., 1999), which might provide a clear and strong streptavidin labeling at the apicoplast (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: TurboID proved to be a reasonably robust approach for the identification of putative apicoplast transporters.
source: Collectively, TurboID proved to be a reasonably robust approach for the identification of putative apicoplast transporters.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the screening results.

claim: Proteins with conserved transport domains are mostly conserved in the Apicomplexa.
source: The conservation heatmap showed that proteins with conserved transport domains (HAP1, 3, 4, 9, 10, 28, 33, 34, 41, and 50) are mostly conserved in the Apicomplexa (Figure 2A), including the Gregarina and Cryptosporidium that have lost the apicoplast.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by conservation heatmap data in Figure 2A.

claim: Most orthologs with the exception of HAP3 and HAP4 can be identified in green algae, red algae, and plants.
source: Further analysis revealed that most orthologs with the exception of HAP3 and HAP4, can be identified in green algae, red algae, and plants (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by conservation heatmap data in Figure 2B.

claim: The red alga is considered to have given rise to the ancestor of the secondary plastid.
source: As the red alga is considered to have given rise to the ancestor of the secondary plastid (Gould et al., 2008; Janouskovec et al., 2010), the results thus indicated that those transporters were possibly derived from the red alga.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: Several transporters are predicted to be essential in T. gondii and in P. falciparum.
source: Several transporters, such as HAP1, 3, 4, and 34 and 50, are predicted to be essential in T. gondii and in P. falciparum (Figure 2A, B, and Supplementary file 3a contains the P. falciparum orthologs with fitness scores) (Sidik et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations and shown in Figure 2A, B.

claim: Three of the essential transporters (HAP1, 3, and 4) belong to the MFS.
source: The analyses with InterProScan showed that three of these transporters (HAP1, 3, and 4) belong to the MFS (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by domain analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The MFS is a large family of transporters capable of transporting small solutes in response to chemiosmotic ion gradients.
source: The MFS is a large family of transporters capable of transporting small solutes in response to chemiosmotic ion gradients (Pao et al., 1998; Walmsley et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: These MFS transporters contain a pair of MCT with 11–12 TMDs.
source: These MFS transporters contain a pair of MCT with 11–12 TMDs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by topology analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The MCTs play essential roles in the transport of nutrients, such as pyruvate, lactate, amino acids in the plasma membrane of human cells.
source: The MCTs play essential roles in the transport of nutrients, such as pyruvate, lactate, amino acids and so on, in the plasma membrane of human cells (Felmlee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The two transporters AMT1 and AMT2 are absent in red algae, green algae, and plants.
source: We noticed that these two transporters are absent in red algae, green algae, and plants (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by conservation heatmap data in Figure 2B.

claim: APT1 was identifiable in primary plastid-containing taxa (e.g. plants) but not in cyanobacteria.
source: This observation is in contrast to APT1, which was identifiable in these primary plastid-containing taxa (e.g. plants) but not in cyanobacteria (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by conservation heatmap data in Figure 2B.

claim: The plant orthologs of APT1 are derived from a putative host cell that previously engulfed a cyanobacteria.
source: Evolution and phylogenetic analyses suggested that the plant orthologs of APT1 are derived from a putative host cell that previously engulfed a cyanobacteria (Knappe et al., 2003; Weber et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: The AMTs were identifiable in the photosynthetic relative (e.g. Chromera velia) of the apicomplexans, and a distant relative taxa of Oomycetes.
source: The AMTs were identifiable in the photosynthetic relative (e.g. Chromera velia) of the apicomplexans, and a distant relative taxa of Oomycetes (Figure 2A), indicating a broader conservation in these species.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by conservation heatmap data in Figure 2A.

claim: Most species contain at least two identifiable orthologs of AMTs, including Crytosporidium spp.
source: We further analyzed orthologs in selected species of apicomplexans and found that most species contain at least two identifiable orthologs, including Crytosporidium spp. (Supplementary file 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on ortholog analysis.

claim: The pair of AMTs is likely to have critical roles in metabolic integration of the endosymbiont in the parasite cytosol during evolution.
source: Collectively, the pair of AMTs is likely to have critical roles in metabolic integration of the endosymbiont in the parasite cytosol during evolution.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the conservation analysis.

claim: The putative transporters AMT1 and AMT2 are highly likely to be localized at the apicoplast membranes.
source: The confocal imaging showed that AMT1-6Ty was almost perfectly co-localized with AMT2-6HA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that the putative transporters are highly likely to be localized at the apicoplast membranes.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The precise topology of AMT1 and AMT2 within the apicoplast membranes merits future investigation.
source: Due to the complexity of the apicoplast membranes, and heterogeneity of immunolabeling, the precise topology of AMT1 and AMT2 within the apicoplast membranes merits future investigation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section identifying a limitation.

claim: The processing and topology of AMTs is complex and unpredictable in T. gondii.
source: The processing and topology of AMTs is complex and unpredictable in T. gondii, thus requiring further work to clarify the origin of either the processing hypothesis, alternative splicing, or alternative initiator codons in the parasite.
evidence: This is stated in the results section identifying a limitation.

claim: The AID fusions were correctly localized to the apicoplast and were depleted within 24 hr of IAA treatment.
source: Further analysis by IFA showed that the AID fusions were correctly localized to the apicoplast and were depleted within 24 hr of IAA treatment (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2); however, the parasite bodies were morphologically normal.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by IFA data in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The parasite bodies were morphologically normal after 24 hr of IAA treatment.
source: Further analysis by IFA showed that the AID fusions were correctly localized to the apicoplast and were depleted within 24 hr of IAA treatment (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2); however, the parasite bodies were morphologically normal.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on IFA observations.

claim: The AMTs are potentially essential for in vitro parasite growth.
source: In summary, the AMTs are potentially essential for in vitro parasite growth.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the plaque assay data.

claim: Depletion of the transporters caused strong growth defects and delayed death of the parasites.
source: These results suggested that depletion of the transporters caused strong growth defects and delayed death of the parasites.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on replication assay data.

claim: Depletion of the AMTs caused swelling or breakdown of the apicoplast in the intracellular or extracellular parasites.
source: This observation suggested swelling or breakdown of the apicoplast in the intracellular or extracellular parasites depleted with the AMTs, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on ACP diffusion observations.

claim: The ACP diffusion gradually increased while comparing the three cycles for the same AID line in both the intracellular and extracellular parasites.
source: Detailed analysis of the phenotypes showed that the ACP diffusion gradually increased while comparing the three cycles for the same AID line in both the intracellular and extracellular parasites (Figure 3G, H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by ACP diffusion data in Figure 3G, H.

claim: Further depletion of AMT1-AID had no further effect on ACP diffusion beyond AMT2-AID depletion.
source: These results suggested that depletion of AMT2-AID resulted in much more severe defects (swelling or breakdown) of the apicoplast than that of AMT1-AID, and further depletion of AMT1-AID had no further effect.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on ACP diffusion analysis.

claim: Measuring the endocytic trafficking of GFP vesicles in parasites in the absence/presence of atorvastatin could reflect levels of protein prenylation and isoprenoids (IPP).
source: Therefore, measuring the endocytic trafficking of GFP vesicles in parasites in the absence/presence of atorvastatin could reflect levels of protein prenylation and isoprenoids (IPP).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as the rationale for the GFP acquisition assay.

claim: The substrates modified at the proteins were mainly derived from the apicoplast biosynthesis pathway – the MEP pathway.
source: The substrates modified at the proteins were mainly derived from the apicoplast biosynthesis pathway – the MEP pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as background knowledge.

claim: The IPP synthesis is significantly decreased in the AID lines depleted with the transporters.
source: These results altogether thus suggested that the IPP synthesis is significantly decreased in the AID lines depleted with the transporters.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the GFP acquisition assay.

claim: Depletions of AMT1 and AMT2 resulted in similar levels of IPP reduction in parasites at 12 hr of IAA induction.
source: However, it was noteworthy that parasites depleted with AMT1-AID and AMT2-AID had similar levels of reduced GFP transport and parasites with reduced protein abundance of Rab1B at the 12 hr of IAA induction, suggesting that depletions of AMT1 and AMT2 resulted in similar levels of IPP reduction in parasites.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on GFP transport and Rab1B analysis.

claim: A reduced level of mitochondrial membrane potential was detected in the AMT1-AID or AMT2-AID lines grown in IAA for 24 hr.
source: This was further manifested by a reduced level of mitochondrial membrane potential detected by mitotracker red in the AMT1-AID or AMT2-AID lines grown in IAA for 24 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by mitotracker data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: IPP is the precursor for synthesis of ubiquinone, an essential electron carrier required for electron transport in the mitochondria.
source: IPP is the precursor for synthesis of ubiquinone, an essential electron carrier required for electron transport in the mitochondria (Kennedy et al., 2019b; Sleda et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: The metabolomics detected 66 metabolites in total in the TIR1 and AID lines.
source: The metabolomics detected 66 metabolites in total in these lines (Supplementary file 4a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the metabolomics data.

claim: 15, 23, and 34 differential metabolites were identified in the parasite groups depleted with either AMT1-AID, AMT2-AID, or both (dKD).
source: After analyses using Dunnett's multiple comparison methods, 15, 23, and 34 differential metabolites were identified in the parasite groups depleted with either AMT1-AID, AMT2-AID, or both (dKD) (Supplementary file 4b), in comparison with TIR1.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the metabolomics analysis.

claim: Inactivated FASII proteins led to reduced synthesis of fatty acids up to 18 carbons long.
source: These results were consistent with previous studies where inactivated FASII proteins led to reduced synthesis of fatty acids up to 18 carbons long, and exogenous additions of the C14 and C16 fatty acids could complement growth defects (Liang et al., 2020; Ramakrishnan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: Exogenous additions of the C14 and C16 fatty acids could complement growth defects caused by inactivated FASII proteins.
source: These results were consistent with previous studies where inactivated FASII proteins led to reduced synthesis of fatty acids up to 18 carbons long, and exogenous additions of the C14 and C16 fatty acids could complement growth defects (Liang et al., 2020; Ramakrishnan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: Lipids can be partially acquired from the host cells.
source: Studies suggested that lipids can be partially acquired from the host cells (Krishnan et al., 2020), which includes those in the endocytic vesicles (Koreny et al., 2023; Wan et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: The endocytic vesicles containing GFP were diffused in the parasite cytosol, indicating that the host cell-derived lipids were not affected in the protein-depleted parasites.
source: Here, we observed that the endocytic vesicles containing GFP were diffused in the parasite cytosol, indicating that the host cell-derived lipids were not affected in the protein-depleted parasites.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the GFP acquisition assay.

claim: An overall trend toward lower levels of myristic acid, palmitoleic acid, and trans-oleic acid was observed in AMT2-AID and tKD parasites in comparison with the AMT1-AID parasites.
source: In contrast to the same level of reduced endocytic trafficking of GFP vesicles in the AID lines, an overall trend toward lower levels of myristic acid (C14 fatty acid), palmitoleic acid (C16 fatty acid), and trans-oleic acid (C18 fatty acid) was observed in AMT2-AID and tKD parasites in comparison with the AMT1-AID parasites (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by metabolomics data in Figure 4E.

claim: These results supported the notion of a stronger impairment of the FASII pathway in parasites depleted with AMT2-AID.
source: These results supported the notion of a stronger impairment of the FASII pathway in parasites depleted with AMT2-AID.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the metabolomics data.

claim: Defective membrane potential was likely caused by a reduced supply of IPP for synthesis of ubiquinone or synthesis of heme.
source: This would likely result from defective membrane potential caused by a reduced supply of IPP for synthesis of ubiquinone, as described above, or synthesis of heme that requires co-operation between the mitochondrion and the apicoplast (Harding et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Creatine and lactic acid were likely associated with reduced metabolic levels in the parasites.
source: Another two metabolites, creatine and lactic acid, were likely associated with reduced metabolic levels in the parasites (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by metabolomics data in Figure 4E.

claim: Pyruvate was not identified in the untargeted metabolomics as it is actually a product of glycolysis in the cytosol.
source: The untargeted metabolomics tends to identify differential metabolites by comparing the AID to TIR1 lines. Pyruvate was not identified, as it is actually a product of glycolysis in the cytosol.
evidence: This is stated in the results section explaining a limitation of the metabolomics approach.

claim: The transporters are expectedly associated with the MEP and FASII pathways, to support synthesis of IPP and FA in the apicoplast.
source: Collectively, the transporters are expectedly associated with the MEP and FASII pathways, to support synthesis of IPP and FA in the apicoplast.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the metabolomics data.

claim: Depletion of AMT2 resulted in stronger defects on ACP diffusion and synthesis of fatty acids, suggesting a more important role of AMT2 in the apicoplast.
source: Depletion of AMT2 resulted in stronger defects on ACP diffusion and synthesis of fatty acids, suggesting a more important role of AMT2 in the apicoplast.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the comparative phenotypic data.

claim: There was no obvious change to protein levels in the 6HA fusions in the AID-Ty lines after IAA induction for 36 hr.
source: After IAA induction for 36 hr, we did not see obvious changes to protein levels in the 6HA fusions in the AID-Ty lines on western blots and IFA (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot and IFA data in Figure 5A, B.

claim: ACC1 was gone in some parasites within a single vacuole in the AMT2-AID-depleted parasites, where ACP was clearly stained with a slight diffusion.
source: Further analysis showed that ACC1 was gone in some parasites within a single vacuole in the AMT2-AID-depleted parasites, where ACP was clearly stained with a slight diffusion (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by IFA data in Figure 5D.

claim: Several attempts to delete ACC1 failed in the study.
source: Several attempts to delete ACC1 failed in our study, supporting a critical role of ACC1 in the FASII process.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing experimental attempts.

claim: ACC1 has a critical role in the FASII process.
source: Several attempts to delete ACC1 failed in our study, supporting a critical role of ACC1 in the FASII process.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the failed deletion attempts.

claim: The observation of ACC1 loss supports stronger phenotypes in AMT2-AID-depleted parasites.
source: Thus, the observation of ACC1 loss supports stronger phenotypes in AMT2-AID-depleted parasites.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the ACC1 data.

claim: Depletion of the AMTs caused an initially gradual defect, but then a much more focused sharper defect in parasite replication in the 3rd 24 hr.
source: In addition, depletion of the AMTs caused an initially gradual defect, but then a much more focused sharper defect in parasite replication in the 3rd 24 hr and showed a delayed death phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the replication phenotype.

claim: Depletion of the AMTs showed a delayed death phenotype.
source: In addition, depletion of the AMTs caused an initially gradual defect, but then a much more focused sharper defect in parasite replication in the 3rd 24 hr and showed a delayed death phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the replication phenotype.

claim: Parasite replication exhibited gradual decreases upon depletion of TPC and APT1 by utilization of the tetracyclin-inducible system (TATi).
source: Previous studies showed that parasite replication exhibited gradual deceases upon depletion of TPC and APT1 by utilization of a low efficient knockdown strategy – the tetracyclin-inducible system (TATi) (Brooks et al., 2010; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: The apicoplast numbers identified by TEM dropped in the AMT1-AID parasites when induced for 24 and 36 hr.
source: This examination showed that the apicoplast numbers identified by TEM dropped in the AMT1-AID parasites, when induced for 24 and 36 hr, and the numbers dropped by much greater levels in the AMT2-AID parasites, following 12 hr of IAA induction (Figure 6B).

claim: The apicoplast numbers dropped by much greater levels in the AMT2-AID parasites following 12 hr of IAA induction.
source: This examination showed that the apicoplast numbers identified by TEM dropped in the AMT1-AID parasites, when induced for 24 and 36 hr, and the numbers dropped by much greater levels in the AMT2-AID parasites, following 12 hr of IAA induction (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by TEM quantification data in Figure 6B.

claim: The apicoplast was identified only 3 times in the AMT2-AID parasites at 36 hr induction.
source: Notably, the apicoplast was identified only 3 times in the AMT2-AID parasites at 36 hr induction.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the TEM quantification.

claim: The percentage of the abnormal apicoplast increased for both of the AID lines.
source: Accordingly, the percentage of the abnormal apicoplast increased for both of the AID lines.

claim: Depletion of AMT2-AID resulted in much higher levels of abnormal apicoplasts at the three induction time points, compared to those in parasites depleted with AMT1-AID.

claim: The mouse sera clearly recognized proteins of the parasitophorous vacuoles of the parasites.
source: The IFA showed that the mouse sera clearly recognized proteins of the parasitophorous vacuoles of the parasites (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by IFA data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The strong growth impairment conferred by AMT1 depletion in parasites in cell culture surprisingly resulted in only reduced parasite virulence in mice.
source: However, the strong growth impairment conferred by AMT1 depletion in parasites in cell culture surprisingly resulted in only reduced parasite virulence in mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the discrepancy between in vitro and in vivo results.

claim: The discrepancy between in vitro and in vivo results is related to the relatively modest defects observed in the AMT1-depleted parasites.
source: We assume that this discrepancy is related to the relatively modest defects, such as the ACP diffusion/apicoplast abnormality (revealed by TEM)/FASII activity, as observed in the AMT1-depleted parasites.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as speculation about the discrepancy.

claim: The remaining apicoplast is still functionally generating an adequate amount of metabolites, allowing the parasites to survive in mice.
source: Thus, the remaining apicoplast is still functionally generating an adequate amount of metabolites, allowing the parasites to survive in mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as speculation about the discrepancy.

claim: The discrepancy is possibly associated with different transport capabilities of substrates by AMT1 and AMT2.
source: However, the discrepancy is possibly associated with different transport capabilities of substrates by AMT1 and AMT2.

claim: Weaker phenotypes in AMT1-depleted parasites argue for the possibility of different transport capabilities.
source: Though this does not perfectly explain the discrepancy, weaker phenotypes in AMT1-depleted parasites argue for this possibility.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as speculation about the discrepancy.

claim: Phenotypic outcomes did not result from apicoplast abnormality since other phenotypic outcomes were more severe in the AMT2-depleted parasites.
source: We also observed similar phenotypes reflecting decreased levels of the MEP biosynthesis activity upon depletion of AMT1 and AMT2, indicating that phenotypic outcomes did not result from apicoplast abnormality, since other phenotypic outcomes were more severe in the AMT2-depleted parasites.
evidence: This is stated in the limitations section as an interpretation of the phenotypic data.

claim: Metabolic defects possibly result from a reduced supply of substrates by each of the transporter.
source: We predict, therefore, that the metabolic defects possibly result from a reduced supply of substrates by each of the transporter.
evidence: This is stated in the limitations section as speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Metabolic defects in TPC- and APT1-depleted parasites were possibly caused by pleiotropic effects of apicoplast loss.
source: However, these phenotypes were possibly caused by pleiotropic effects of apicoplast loss, since they were analyzed by a comparably slow inactivation system to deplete the transporters of TPC and APT1 (with an induction of at least 3–4 days).

claim: The effect of apicoplast loss on phenotypic results caused by depletion of the AMTs cannot be excluded.
source: Nevertheless, in our case with a highly efficient inactivation system, we still cannot exclude the effect of apicoplast loss on phenotypic results caused by depletion of the AMTs.
evidence: This is stated in the limitations section identifying a limitation.

claim: A more precise understanding of the functions of the AMTs will require further identification of the topology, protein interactions and substrate transport capability.
source: Therefore, a more precise understanding of the functions of the AMTs will require further identification of the topology, protein interactions and substrate transport capability in the complex configuration of the apicoplast membranes.
evidence: This is stated in the limitations section identifying future directions.

claim: The application of more sophisticated approaches may enable tackling the important question of substrate transport by AMT1 and AMT2.
source: Thereafter, the application of more sophisticated approaches, such as Xenopus oocytes, an improved E. coli system, or a yeast expression system, may enable us to tackle the important question of substrate transport by AMT1 and AMT2.
evidence: This is stated in the limitations section identifying future directions.

claim: Future progress will shed critical insights into the discrepancies in parasite growth when comparing cell culture versus infections in mice.
source: Future progress in this direction will thus shed critical insights into the discrepancies in parasite growth that we observe when comparing cell culture versus infections in mice.
